title: Multi-argument function call as argument to another function
description:
Here are two examples (based on first example from documentation for `case_when()`):
```
# Bad?
tibble(int = 1:70) |> 
  mutate(
    response = case_when(
      int %% 35 == 0 ~ "fizz buzz",
      int %% 5 == 0 ~ "fizz",
      int %% 7 == 0 ~ "buzz",
      .default = as.character(int)
    )
  )
```

```
# Good?
tibble(int = 1:70) |> 
  mutate(
    response = 
      case_when(
        int %% 35 == 0 ~ "fizz buzz",
        int %% 5 == 0 ~ "fizz",
        int %% 7 == 0 ~ "buzz",
        .default = as.character(int)
      )
  )
```

In the first case, the name `response`obscures the fact that the arguments that follow belong to `case_when()`.  This becomes much worse as the number of arguments and levels of nesting increase, so I would far prefer
```
    response = 
      case_when(
```
to
```
    response = case_when(
```
Thoughts?  Could this be added to the guide?

title: Discourage <<- ?
description:
{lintr} has long discouraged `<<-` as a default "undesirable operator":

https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/50d9430173a9ed07570956e2a1de01c82fea9d93/R/zzz.R#L218-L223

Somehow I'd thought the Tidyverse guide also makes this ruling, but just found myself checking & realized there's no opinion.

I think avoiding `<<-` is good practice. The picture-perfect ideal usage looks like this:

```r
w <- e <- NULL
tryCatch(
  foo(),
  warning = \(c) w <<- c,
  error = \(c) e <<- c
)
```

Here the target of `<<-` is maximally close in the code to where `<<-` is used. In any other case, it starts requiring a large mental load on the code reader to keep track of in which environment the LHS of `<<-` actually ends up getting assigned, and mistakes can cause really unexpected and hard-to-debug behavior (`x <<- ...`, where we meant `y <<- ...`, might wind up wiping out something important in some other environment).

These days I strongly encourage authors to be sometimes painfully explicit instead:

```r
w <- e <- NULL
env <- environment()
tryCatch(
  foo(),
  warning = \(c) env$w <- c,
  error = \(c) env$e <- c
)
```

The code is slightly messier (we often wind up needing many more `env$` qualifiers) but often easier to understand and maintain.

PS
The guide _used to_ discourage pipe "in-place" assignment operator `%<>%`:

https://github.com/tidyverse/style/blob/8de4bbcbfb79220cdbfb8714298a9d13f18e9967/pipes.Rmd#L129

This advice was thrown out along with the move to _only_ use the native pipe `|>` (#225). I believe the motivation for that advice would be similar to the proposed ruling here.

title: Moving towards {package} for package naming
description:
The current recommendation is to use **package** on first usage, then just package I believe, or just package (Reference: https://github.com/tidyverse/style/issues/50). To me, it makes perfect sense because it won't be confused with `code_we <- write` or `pkg::fun()`, yet {package} stands out from normal text with a unique visual signature, without conflicting with common usage of *italics*, **bold** or "quoted".

```R
)
```

But I think I now prefer keeping each argument on its own line:

```R
  extra_argument_a = 10,

)
```

title: Clarify empty braced statements
description:
The guide currently has pretty broad rules about braces:

https://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#indenting

One edge case apparently precluded by the current rules is an empty expression: `{ }` or `{}`, for example empty while loops:

```
while (some_updating_condition()) { }
```

I don't think splitting the braces is a good choice in this case:

```
while (some_updating_condition()) {
}
```

`styler` already enforces what looks to me like a good rule:

```
library(styler)

style_text("while (TRUE) { }")
# while (TRUE) { }
style_text("while (TRUE) {}")
# while (TRUE) {}
style_text("while (TRUE) { 1 }")
# while (TRUE) {
#   1
# }
```

Is it worth codifying this behavior in the guide?

We are wondering how to handle this in `lintr`: https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/issues/1346

title: Clarify indentation rules if multiple apply at the same time
description:
Raised in https://github.com/r-lib/styler/issues/1065

There are circumstances where both, a hanging / block indent for a function call and a block indent for line continuation of binary operators (e.g. pipes), are triggered on the same line of code.
Currently, lintr's `indentation_linter()` requires two levels of indent in such cases whereas styler only wants one.

Here are some code examples that need clarification on what the tidyverse style should be:

```r
# multi-line if condition
if (long_conditional &&
      other_long_conditional) {
  conditionally_evaluated_code()
}
# vs.
if (long_conditional &&
  other_long_conditional) {
  conditionally_evaluated_code()
}

# multi-line if condition with pipe
if (long_conditional |>
    long_computation() |>
    other_long_computation()) {
  conditionally_evaluated_code()
}
# vs.
if (long_conditional |>
  long_computation() |>
  other_long_computation()) {
  conditionally_evaluated_code()
}

# (assuming hanging indent is allowed for function calls too)
# multi-line function call
fun(arg1 &&
      still_arg1,
    arg2)
# vs.
fun(arg1 &&
    still_arg1,
    arg2)

# multi-line function call with pipe
fun(arg1 |>
      arg1_processor1() |>
      arg1_processor2(),
    arg2)
# vs.
fun(arg1 |>
    arg1_processor1() |>
    arg1_processor2(),
    arg2)
```

cc @IndrajeetPatil, @lorenzwalthert

title: Rules for shorthand lambda \() ?
description:
I have been trying to incorporate `\()` into code more and wonder if the style guide would benefit from including some do's/don'ts about using it. For example, here are some rough rules I've been following:

 - Use `\()` if and only if the function body fits on the same line (i.e., never use `\()` with a `{`-wrapped body)
 - Avoid using `\()` when assigning a function, i.e. rarely use `foo <- \(...)` [not prohibited since there are some cases where we can _just_ squeeze a short wrapper function into one <=80-character line with `\()`, but using `function()` would require ballooning the  definition to three lines to accommodate the `{`]
 - Prefer using `\()` with 0 or 1 arguments, occasionally 2, and rarely with `...` unless it's the only argument
 - Avoid the parentheses-dense usage inside a pipe like `x |> (\(...) ...)()`

title: Allow in-line switch
description:
Current advice in the guide prevents statements like the following:

```
units_power <- switch(suffix, k = 1, m = 2, g = 3, t = 4, p = 5)
```

I think the alternative wastes a lot of real estate:

```
units_power <- switch(suffix,
  k = 1,
  m = 2,
  g = 3,
  t = 4,
  p = 5
)
```

The current examples don't address this case specifically... the `good` example has a fall-through stop, in which case keeping it on its own line is similar to the `Control flow` recommendations. And once _one_ argument gets its own line, I agree all should.

But also as mentioned, lacking a fall-through stop is OK if the input has been validated (e.g. with `match.arg()`).

The other non-positional `bad` examples use fall-through; I agree on using new lines in the fall-through case as well, since it's visually clearer.

That leaves an example like mine: (1) input is pre-validated, so we don't need a fall-through; and (2) all arguments get values.

title: Need clarity on named vs. unnamed arguments and line breaks
description:
In #39 we have [this quote](https://github.com/tidyverse/style/issues/39#issuecomment-324352762):

> If no arguments are named, and it doesn't fit on one line.then each argument always gets its own line.

Downthread it's pointed out this is not very clear in the style guide as of now.

I'd also like to point out that I find it to be less-than-optimal advice. This came up in {lintr} here, where we have:

https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/pull/2543/files#diff-f32b4985bf0c6dd105640050567eb5e0d6d097c1e6e365a69a0e5a4c24dc2b13R40

```r
conds <- c(conds,
  "self::OP-RIGHT-PAREN[preceding-sibling::*[not(self::COMMENT)][1][self::OP-LEFT-PAREN or self::OP-COMMA]]"
)
```

I think it's **very good** to put `conds` on the same line as `c(` here because it makes it _very clear_ we're overwriting the same object in a way that's not as transparent if we force `conds` to come on the next line.

Our usage is also in line with the current style guide, but not the text of the issue linked, so I'm hoping this discussion can be revisited.

title: Advice for long formulas
description:
Is there any advice we want to encode for long formulas?

Currently the guide only discusses formulas w.r.t. operator spacing, and only in the context of one-sided formulas:

https://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#infix-operators

It's quite common for us to see formulas stretch >1 line, even up to 4-5 lines or more. I am not sure what rules to apply for best readability in this case.

 1. Should a terminal `~` always induce indentation (so that the RHS is always outdented vs. the LHS)?
 2. Should a terminal `+` (or occasionally `-`) induce indentation on the next line?

Originally raised here: https://github.com/r-lib/styler/issues/900

Key example -- how should the following be formatted (as might come up, e.g., in a `dcast()` reshaping):

```
long_y_variable1 + long_y_variable_2 +
  long_y_variable_3 ~
    long_x_variable_1 + long_x_variable_2 +
      long_x_variable_3
```

Can any of those outdentations be removed?

Perhaps the problem is more generally about which operators do/don't induce indentation on the next line -- currently there's no discussion of long arithmetic statements either. It seems to me splitting on higher-precedence operators is a good general rule (so split on `+`, not `*`, where possible).

title: Indents - is 2 spaces really good?
description:
https://github.com/tidyverse/style/blob/fbdebd8858baf7a273ab6cd78237484ef03478cb/syntax.Rmd#L288C1-L289C49

Is there a reason why 2 space indents is considered good when the published [R coding standard recommends 4?](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-ints.html#R-coding-standards). 2 spaces would also seem to go against the convention of most other languages and accepted practices. Under normal settings 2 Spaces also goes against pretty well established indent conventions from the print industry (based on literally centuries worth of reading ergonomics learning). Basically it seems like there are number of good reasons to make recommended default indents 4 or more spaces rather than 2.

It might be nice to have a discussion about this as the default goes against conventional wisdom and can cause readability and accessibility issues. At the very least it might be nice to have a documented explanation as to why broader indent conventions are being diverged from in tidyverse.

title: return() in pipes should go on its own line
description:
This is closely related to the inline statements section:

https://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#inline-statements

> Function calls that affect control flow (like `return()`, `stop()` or `continue`) should always go in their own `{}` block

`return()` should never be inlined in a pipe:

```
x %>% foo() %>% bar() %>% return()
```

should always be

```
x %>%
  foo() %>%
  bar() %>%
  return()
```

Does this belong better in the cited section, or in the section on pipes (e.g. https://style.tidyverse.org/pipes.html#short-pipes)?

title: Enforce variable desambiguation in style
description:
Hi, 

The name collision might cause mistakes when using pipes or some tidyverse functions.

In general, I would suggest the use of `.data` and `.env` to be added in style recommandation.

I would also suggest the use of `dplyr::across` and `tidyselect` for the `dplyr::group_by` or similar features.

Below are examples:

```R
################################################################################

library(magrittr)

alphabet<- tibble::tibble(
  rank= seq_len(26),
  letter= c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", "g", "h", "i", "j", "k", "l", "m", 
    "n", "o", "p", "q", "r", "s", "t", "u", "v", "w", "x","y", "z"),
  type = factor(c("v", "c", "c", "c", "v", "c", "c", "c", "v", "c", "c", "c",
    "c", "c", "v", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "v", "c", "c", "c", "v", "c"))
)

rank <- 5
letter = "type"

# BAD

# 1
dplyr::filter(alphapet, rank <= rank)

# 2
dplyr::group_by(alphabet, type) %>% dplyr::group_by(letter) %>% dplyr::count()


# GOOD

# 1
dplyr::filter(alphabet, .data$rank <= .env$rank)

# 2
dplyr::group_by(alphabet, type) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(
    dplyr::across(tidyselect::all_of(.env$letter)
  )
) %>%
  dplyr::count()

```

title: Column names in join calls - to include or not to include?
description:
I was answering a question on StackOverflow, and I got a comment from a more senior user saying that "it's a good habit to explicitly specify which columns are joined by". I thought I would check the style guide, and to my surprise, it had nothing to say about it (nor did any other R style guide I could find, for that matter).

In a circumstance such as:

```
df1 <- tibble(
    Country = c("France", "Spain", "England")
)

df2 <- tibble(
    Country = rep(c("France", "Spain", "England"), each = 2),
    League = c("Ligue 1", "Ligue 2", "Liga", "Liga 2", "PL1", "PL2")
)
```
You could join with a `by = "Country"`, or without one, it has the same result. 

I was wondering if this has come up before, or if not, if there is some kind of stance on it. Many thanks!

title: Use and recommend the base pipe
Disagreement with styler and lintr about long lines. Rstudio gives a better format.
description:
Hi! 

I have this problem. Suppose you have this long line in your code:

```
value <- my_function(arg0 = 0, arg1 = 1, arg2 = 2, arg3 = 3, arg4 = 4, arg5 = 5, arg6 = 6, arg7 = 7)
```

Checking it with `styler`, returns the unmodified string. 
```r
styler::style_text("value <- my_function(arg0 = 0, arg1 = 1, arg2 = 2, arg3 = 3, arg4 = 4, arg5 = 5, arg6 = 6, arg7 = 7)")
value <- my_function(arg0 = 0, arg1 = 1, arg2 = 2, arg3 = 3, arg4 = 4, arg5 = 5, arg6 = 6, arg7 = 7)
```
However, `lintr` is complaining about the length of the line
```
[line_length_linter]: Lines should not be more than 80 characters. This line is 100 characters.	
```

In my opinion, Rstudio gives a better format: 
```r
value <-
  my_function(
    arg0 = 0,
    arg1 = 1,
    arg2 = 2,
    arg3 = 3,
    arg4 = 4,
    arg5 = 5,
    arg6 = 6,
    arg7 = 7
  )
```


What can I do to make `styler` behave like Rstudio in this case? 

Best.

title: Formating of function arguments behaviour changes if `indent_by` is not `2`
description:
Problem: Changing `indent_by` configuration doesn't implement the same styling guides _(on "Double-indent")_

It changes the style to "Function-indent" ([reference](https://style.tidyverse.org/functions.html#long-lines-1))

Reproducible code:

``` r
foo_2 <- "foo <- function(
    bar) {
  NULL
}"

foo_4 <- "foo <- function(
        bar) {
    NULL
}"

styler::style_text(foo_2)
#> foo <- function(
#>     bar) {
#>   NULL
#> }
styler::style_text(foo_4, indent_by = 4L)
#> foo <- function(bar) {
#>     NULL
#> }
styler::style_text(foo_4, transformers = styler::tidyverse_style(indent_by = 4))
#> foo <- function(bar) {
#>     NULL
#> }

testthat::expect_identical(
    foo_2 |> 
        styler::style_text(transformers = styler::tidyverse_style(indent_by = 2L)) |> 
        as.character() |> 
        paste(collapse = "\n", sep = ""),
    foo_2
)

testthat::expect_identical(
    foo_4 |> 
        styler::style_text(transformers = styler::tidyverse_style(indent_by = 4)) |> 
        as.character() |> 
        paste(collapse = "\n", sep = ""),
    foo_4
)
#> Error: paste(...) not identical to `foo_4`.
#> 1/1 mismatches
#> x[1]: "foo <- function(bar) {\n    NULL\n}"
#> y[1]: "foo <- function(\n        bar) {\n    NULL\n}"
```

title: Keyword arguments -- to quote or not to quote
description:
We recently started enforcing a rule that named arguments should only be quoted when required, e.g.

```
# bad
c("a" = 1, "b" = 2, "an elephant" = 3)

# good
c(a = 1, b = 2, "an elephant" = 3)
```

However, some small pushback we got referenced some tidyverse manuals, e.g.:

 - https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/plyr/versions/1.8.6/topics/rename uses `rename(mtcars, c("disp" = "displacement"))`
 - https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/join.html uses `band_members %>% full_join(band_instruments2, by = c("name" = "artist"))`

R cannot tell the difference between the two:

```
identical(
  parse(text = 'c(a = "b")', keep.source = FALSE),
  parse(text = 'c("a" = "b")', keep.source = FALSE)
)
# [1] TRUE
```

But given the examples in the documentation, I am wondering whether this is an unwritten rule, and if so, could we explicate it (it only applies to joins? renames?)

title: Proposal: Don't use & or | in if (should be && and ||)
description:
Statements like

```
if (x & y) ...
```

Are prone to error when `length(x)>1` or `length(y)>1` (the mistaken case can be caught with the recent R environment variable `_R_CHECK_LENGTH_1_LOGIC2_`).

It's also less efficient to use `&` when `&&` is appropriate.

The same applies to `||` and `while`.

Vector versions can apply within the condition statement, inside an aggregator:

```
if (x && any(y | z))
```

title: Allowing call-like function definitions if delineated properly
description:
Filed first as https://github.com/r-lib/styler/issues/829, but in writing that I realized the style guide itself could weigh in here as well.

Currently in the style guide we have (https://style.tidyverse.org/functions.html#long-lines-1):

```
# Bad
long_function_name <- function(a = "a long argument",
  b = "another argument",
  c = "another long argument") {
  # Here it's hard to spot where the definition ends and the
  # code begins
}
```

I basically see the point about `c =` having the same indentation as the function body and thus needing to scan for `{` at the end of a line to find the start/end of the definition.

However I think this is nicely avoided by just dropping `) {` to the next line:

```
long_function_name <- function(
  a = "a long argument",
  b = "another argument",
  c = "another long argument"
) {
  # function body
}
```

I would prefer to allow this latter usage, but either weigh it would be helpful for the style guide to be explicit.

title: Match else to the same line as } when present
flexibility of operator spacing / mixing of precedence
description:
I'm not sure how to capture the issue precisely, but I think the current wording of the style guide around operator spacing can lead to some hard-to-read code:

```
a_constant + 1 / 12
```

is IMO pretty hard to read vs

```
a_constant + 1/12
```

I _think_ what's going on here is `+` is lower precedence than `/`, but they have _equal_ spacing. Removing the spacing around `/` is a visual cue about operator precedence.

The logic breaks down when we use more complicated expressions with more than two levels of operator precedence:

```
addend  +  base^exponent / denominator # ??
```

Perhaps the recommendation in this case could be to use parentheses to limit any sub-expression to at most 2 levels of operator precedence. Maybe overkill.

In any case, I think a simple case where `+ | -` and `* | /` are mixed could be spelled out pretty easily.

title: Guidelines for informative error messages
description:
In section 9.1 on error messages, the guide says:

> Use `stop(call. = FALSE), rlang::abort(), Rf_errorcall(R_NilValue, ...)` to avoid cluttering the error message with the name of the function that generated it. That information is often not informative, and can easily be accessed via traceback() or an IDE equivalent.

I disagree that the function name is uninformative, and just wanted to share my two cents on error handling.

I bet many would agree that error handling is one of the most painful parts of working with R. Debugging can take lots of time, and it seems like a really valuable thing to try to improve. In my own experience using packages, the biggest challenge has always been understanding the *context* of the error rather than the nature of the error itself. I'll show what I mean with a simple example, one that follows the guidelines but still results in a confusing error.

In the simplest case, we call a function interactively and get a directly relevant message. It's easy to see what's going on here:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
select(mtcars, nonexistent)
#> Error: Can't subset columns that don't exist.
#> ✖ Column `nonexistent` doesn't exist.
```

<sup>Created on 2020-07-26 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

However, the far more common situation is that the error was thrown from deeper in the call stack:

``` r
obscure_fn()
#> Error: Can't subset columns that don't exist.
#> ✖ Column `nonexistent` doesn't exist.
```

<sup>Created on 2020-07-26 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

This error message is completely uninformative. To understand it, you need to find out where the error is being thrown, so the function name is arguably more important than the message. Unfortunately (and despite what the guide says), the offending function call is *not* easily identifiable from the trace.

``` r
rlang::last_error()
#> <error/vctrs_error_subscript_oob>
#> Can't subset columns that don't exist.
#> ✖ Column `nonexistent` doesn't exist.
#> Backtrace:
#>   1. global::obscure_fn()
#>  22. vctrs:::stop_subscript_oob(...)
#>  23. vctrs:::stop_subscript(...)
#> Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see the full context.
```

The trace claims that `vctrs:::stop_subscript` threw the error, which isn't wrong, but it's misleading. I think the error gets handled in `tidyselect:::eval_select_impl`, but I can only tell by reading the source. If that's true, the error message could easily include "Error in tidyselect::eval_select" along with the other notes. Note that this message plus the `tidyselect::eval_select` documentation are sufficient information to understand exactly what went wrong: I passed some dataframe to `eval_select()`, and it didn't contain the `nonexistent` column.

To actually fix the problem, I need to identify which line in *my* code resulted in selecting the wrong column. This currently requires looking around in the trace. In this (overly simplistic) example, I just need to identify the line `dplyr::select(mtcars, nonexistent)`, which is called from `obscure_fn()`. Since the trace can become cluttered with internal package calls, magrittr/purrr calls, etc, I bet there are ways to improve this aspect of debugging as well.

To summarize:

- I believe it's important to identify the function in the error message. To really understand an error, you need to know which function threw it and what that function does.
- The traceback can get quite complicated with error handling and other calls, and I disagree that contextual info can generally be easily accessed with `traceback()`
- Before you can fix the bug, you need to find the code you wrote that led to the error. This is probably the more complicated problem and maybe out of scope. Is there currently a way to distinguish between the trace from local code — which is both more familiar and more likely to contain the bug — versus package code? Even better, could an error message report the earliest package function call on the path to the error?

title: hard wrap prose at punctuation, otherwise overflow
description:
To meet the 80 character line limit *where possible*, I would suggest to hard wrap prose, such as inside code comments or markdown at (in decreasing order of desirability):

1. Periods `.`
2. Colons `:`
3. Semicolon `;`
3. Commas `,`

If it is not possible, I would suggest allowing overflowing the 80 character limit.

This would be part of the norms of adopting a markdown style guide as per #161.
However, many popular markdown style guides are either silent on the issue, or include several options -- so there's a decision to be made.

My suggestion would be:

```md
<!--Good-->
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consetetur sadipscing elitr, 
sed diam nonumy eirmod tempor invidunt ut labore et dolore magna aliquyam erat, 
sed diam voluptua. 
At vero eos et accusam et justo duo dolores et ea rebum. 
```
(hard wrapping at above punctuation, otherwise overflowing 80 chars)

```md
<!--Also Good-->
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consetetur sadipscing elitr, sed diam nonumy eirmod tempor invidunt ut labore et dolore magna aliquyam erat, sed diam voluptua. 
At vero eos et accusam et justo duo dolores et ea rebum. 
```
(hard wrapping only at periods, otherwise overflowing 80 chars)

```md
<!--Bad-->
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consetetur sadipscing elitr, 
sed diam nonumy eirmod tempor invidunt ut labore et dolore 
magna aliquyam erat, sed diam voluptua. At vero eos et 
accusam et justo duo dolores et ea rebum. 
```
(hard wrapping at 80 chars with no regard to punctuation)

I'd be happy to draft a PR for this, as part of #162.

---

#### Rationale

1. Style guides always attempt to visualise the syntax of the language in question, such as when using vertical alignment around control structures.
    The syntax of natural language is structured by punctuation.
2. Hard wrapping at 80 characters without regard to punctuation can cause confusing `git diff`s.
     For example, some change in line 13 can require require changes in the following lines because due to reflowing the hard breaks.
     In these (frequent) cases, the `git diff`s muddy the intent of the committer.
3. Guaranteed-at-any-cost hard wrapping at 80 characters was necessary for two reasons, which now/here apply to a lesser extend:
     1. Soft wrap wasn't always available. 
         It is now frequently available (editors, IDE, even some `git difftool`s), though admittedly still not everywhere (knitr, terminal).
     2. The overall horizontal organisation of code would be broken by soft wraps.
          This is less of a concern for (markdown) prose, which has little horizontal organisation to begin with.
            Admittedly, there is *some* horizontal organisation in markdown (nested lists) which might look worse when soft wrapped.

These arguments are shared by those (few) markdown style guides which cover the topic at all:

[Arctic Ice Studio](https://arcticicestudio.github.io/styleguide-markdown/rules/whitespace.html#maximum-line-length):

> Therefore, this guide advices to avoid using a character limit per line for flowing text, but try to use a maximum line length of 120 characters (including whitespaces) for all other document elements.

https://github.com/cirosantilli/markdown-style-guide/ (used by GitLab internally, apparently):

> Try to keep lines under 80 characters by breaking large paragraphs logically at points such as:
> - sentences: after a period ., question ? or exclamation mark !
> - clauses: after words like and, which, if ... then, commas ,
> large phrases
>
> It is acceptable to have a line longer than 80 characters, but keep in mind that long sentences are less readable and look worse in tools such as git diff.
>
> Set your editor to wrap lines visually for Markdown in case a large line is present.

I can also think of a **downside**: Hard wrapping at punctuation may conflict with the markdown design principle to be *readable-as-is*.

---

#### Existing Practice in the Tidyverse/r-lib

... is somewhat varied:

Overflowed:

https://github.com/r-lib/roxygen2/blob/b3053b694399416543af877837efb29e6ec34d1f/vignettes/rd.Rmd#L183

Hard-wrapped (to preserve markdown syntax horizontal alignment?)

https://github.com/r-lib/roxygen2/blob/b3053b694399416543af877837efb29e6ec34d1f/vignettes/rd.Rmd#L196-L200

Overflowed (even when there is markdown syntax)

https://github.com/r-lib/roxygen2/blob/b3053b694399416543af877837efb29e6ec34d1f/vignettes/rd.Rmd#L406-L408

title: apply markdown style guide for prose
description:
I'd love some standardisation of how to style markdown in the context of R projects, and packages especially.

Markdown style is orthogonal to styling R, so this may be considered out of scope.
Howeber, I'd suggest that because almost every R project uses markdown in some pretty integral places, some norm for the community might still be helpful.

In decreasing order of applicability, markdown should be styled accordingly in:

1. `*.Rmd` such as in vignettes
2. Roxygen comments, when using markdown syntax.
3. Other comments (only a small subset would apply)

With markdown styling being somewhat orthogonal to rstats, it might be appropriate to just reuse existing style guides, formatters and linters, including:

- [Google](https://github.com/google/styleguide/blob/gh-pages/docguide/style.md)
- [Bitbucket](https://confluence.atlassian.com/bitbucketserver/markdown-syntax-guide-776639995.html)
- [GitLab](https://about.gitlab.com/handbook/markdown-guide/)

*If* there is some interest in standardising on / referring to a markdown style guide inside tidyverse/style, I see these TODOs:

- [ ] choose one of the markdown style guides
- [ ] adapt the style guide where necessary (for example, how to deal with line length https://github.com/tidyverse/style/issues/162)
- [ ] point to / explain rationale for markdown style guide
- [ ] make the source of this repo compliant (to set a good example).
- [ ] choose a recommended linter
- [ ] choose a recommended formatter
- [ ] wrap linter and/or formatter in R package or functions so they can be used conveniently in existing community toolchains.

I'd be happy to draft a PR on this, though I'd need some guidance on which of the existing style guides is most appropriate for the tidyverse community.

title: Sections 2.5 and 3.2 are somewhat contradictory
description:
From [2.5](https://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#long-lines)

> If a function call is too long to fit on a single line, use one line each for the function name, each argument, and the closing `)`. This makes the code easier to read and to change later.

```
# Good
do_something_very_complicated(
  something = "that",
  requires = many,
  arguments = "some of which may be long"
)

# Bad
do_something_very_complicated("that", requires, many, arguments,
                              "some of which may be long"
                              )
```

The `# Bad` example looks a lot like the recommended syntax for long function definitions;

From [3.2](https://style.tidyverse.org/functions.html#long-lines-1)

> If a function definition runs over multiple lines, indent the second line to where the definition starts.

```
# Good
long_function_name <- function(a = "a long argument",
                               b = "another argument",
                               c = "another long argument") {
  # As usual code is indented by two spaces.
}

# Bad
long_function_name <- function(a = "a long argument",
  b = "another argument",
  c = "another long argument") {
  # Here it's hard to spot where the definition ends and the
  # code begins
}
```

I don't think the two recommendations are fundamentally inconsistent, but it would be useful to call out the case of function definitions in 2.5 and/or link to 3.2 from there.

description: The markdown and output of Section 2.5 Long Lines has the text '[Argument names]' which seems to refer to a section that doesn't exist anymore or exists under another name now.

title: (How) should options be documented?
description: I wonder how R options could be documented consistently and if it is worth specifying this in the style guide. For many tidyverse packages such as `{purrr}`, `{tibble}` or `{dplyr}`, I can't quickly find all options documented in one place, e.g. a vignette or help file. Ideally, there would be a consistent name for this, e.g. in `{styler}`, we could call the help file `styler_options` to avoid a helpfile name conflict with `?options`. In my opinion, options are part of the API and should be documented. Maybe this also fits better into r-pkgs, but since there is already a package development section here, I felt I'd open it here.

title: Should warnings and other signals usually have a class?  (And if so, what class name is suggested?)
description:
In sfirke/janitor#452, a discussion of suppressing a specific warning came up.  I know that `rlang::warn()` provides the simple ability to have classed warnings, and I think that for localization support among other reasons, it is likely best practice to give all signals (messages, warnings, and errors) a class to enable easier handling.

I looked into the style guide (https://style.tidyverse.org/error-messages.html), and I didn't see a suggestion for classing signals.  I think that classing signals should be suggested in the guide.  And, if suggested, I think it would help to suggest a class name structure to help give specificity and lack of intersection between class names.

My thought in the janitor issue is the class could be named something like a concatenation of:

* package name
* "signal", "message", "warn", or "error" as applies to the current signal
* function name
* identifier

That should keep it fully specific with effectively zero chance of two signals having overlapping classes.  But, it is a pretty long class name.

title: Should breaking changes have a major version bump?
description:
Under [10.2.3](https://style.tidyverse.org/news.html), breaking changes in the context of `NEWS.md` are discussed. However, it's not stated explicitly that breaking changes require a bump of the major version (e.g. from `1.3.2` to `2.0.0`). It's also not explicitly recommended in [r-pkgs](https://r-pkgs.org/description.html?q=semantic#version) (maybe this issue should rather go there), although semantic versioning is mentioned there. But I think at least for {dplyr} and some other tidyverse packages, I think the convention is to bump the major for breaking changes. Should this be formalised somewhere? I.e. add a sentence here in 

> If there are API breaking changes (as discovered during revdepchecks) these should also appear in their own section at the top. Each bullet should include a description of the symptoms of the change, and what is needed to fix it. The bullet should also be repeated in the appropriate section.

of in r-pkgs.org, e.g. here:

> Increment the development version, e.g. from 9000 to 9001 if you’ve added an important feature that another development package needs to depend on.

Seems to me that how to handle breaking changes in releases is merits more mention than how to increase the dev part of the version when adding new features.

title: What convention for option names should be used?
description:
As with much of base R, the style for global option names is inconsistent. To take a few examples from the [documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/options.html):

```
add.smooth
askYesNo
matprod
PCRE_limit_recursion
```

Within RStudio-adjacent packages, there seems to be a mix of styles (see discussion [here](https://community.rstudio.com/t/name-conventions-for-options/17688))

Jenny Bryan [suggests using `package.option_name`](https://community.rstudio.com/t/name-conventions-for-options/17688/2) as a standard.

Is it worth adding this to the official style guide, for reference, going forward?

title: Re-home "Organising your functions" content from r-pkgs
description: The section "Organising your functions" from the "R code" chapter has been removed, in favour of the treatment of this topic here. However this doesn't seem fully fleshed out here yet. I'm pasting the removed text here, so it can be integrated. --- ## Organising your functions {#r-organising} While you're free to arrange functions into files as you wish, the two extremes are bad: don't put all functions into one file and don't put each function into its own separate file. (It's OK if some files only contain one function, particularly if the function is large or has a lot of documentation.). File names should be meaningful and end in `.R`. ```{r, eval = FALSE} # Good fit_models.R utility_functions.R # Bad foo.r stuff.r ``` Pay attention to capitalization, since you, or some of your collaborators, might be using an operating system with a case-insensitive file system (e.g., Microsoft Windows or OS X). Avoid problems by never using filenames that differ only in capitalisation. My rule of thumb is that if I can't remember the name of the file where a function lives, I need to either separate the functions into more files or give the file a better name. (Unfortunately you can't use subdirectories inside `R/`. The next best thing is to use a common prefix, e.g., `abc-*.R`.). The arrangement of functions within files is less important if you master two important RStudio keyboard shortcuts that let you jump to the definition of a function: * Click a function name in code and press __F2__. * Press __Ctrl + .__ then start typing the name: After navigating to a function using one of these tools, you can go back to where you were by clicking the back arrow at the top-left of the editor or by pressing Ctrl/Cmd-F9.

title: How to reference a family of functions with a shared prefix
description:
Do we have a principle re. where to use an asterisk and/or parentheses when referencing a family of functions (e.g., `rows_` vs. `rows_*()` vs. `rows_*`)? I think the above absence of parentheses is correct because the word "functions" comes after `rows_`, but I want to generalize a rule so we can add it to the style guide.

title: Hyperlinks should always be labelled
description:
Not sure where this goes, but I'm suggesting that hyperlinks should either be naked (e.g. `https://usethis.r-lib.org/articles/articles/pr-functions.html`) or the surrounding prose and link text should make it extremely clear where the hyperlink goes (e.g. "to learn more about blah blah, read the [yada yada vignette](https://usethis.r-lib.org/articles/articles/pr-functions.html)").

Why Your Links Should Never Say "Click Here"

``` r
  1
}

```

description:

https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/24885

It created a bit of a catch 22 with the Apache linter because:

 - `=,` is rejected: no space around an infix
 - `= ,` is rejected: space before a comma

To be clear I'm not sure whether Apache is using the tidyverse style guide.

Nevertheless I tried to find a reference for what the "proper" approach is here and found this style guide is silent on the point... my instinct says `switch` statements are themselves discouraged (or superseded by a `tidyverse` analogue), but in that case I expected to find an explicit discouragement and suggested workaround.

FWIW, I did a rough benchmark and found it 40% faster to leave RHS missing when appropriate:

https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/24885#discussion_r325521563

title: Prefer `return()` over relying on R to implicitly return result
description:
The [section on `return()`](https://style.tidyverse.org/functions.html#return) says:
> Only use return() for early returns. Otherwise, rely on R to return the result of the last evaluated expression.

And has the following (adbridged) example:
```r
# Good
add_two <- function(x, y) {
  x + y
}

# Bad
add_two <- function(x, y) {
  return(x + y)
}
```
Typing less is nice, but our Python colleagues would say:
> Explicit is better than implicit.

Relying on R to return the result of the last evaluated expression *is* explicit, but I think using `return()` is *more* explicit. It's very nice to scan a function definition looking for every instance of `return()` to quickly get an idea of possible outputs.

I considered creating this issue in [tidyverse/principles](https://github.com/tidyverse/principles), as PEP 20 is brought up there, but I stuck with this repo since the guidelines on this topic appear here.

title: Mine "Code style" from r-pkgs for nuggets of wisdom
description:
The section "Code style" from the "R code" chapter has been removed, in favour of the treatment of this topic here. I'm pasting the removed text here, so @Hadley can read it once and make sure all the best parts are, indeed, included here somewhere.

---

## Code style {#style}

Good coding style is like using correct punctuation. You can manage without it, but it sure makes things easier to read. As with styles of punctuation, there are many possible variations. The following guide describes the style that I use (in this book and elsewhere). It is based on Google's [R style guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/Rguide.xml), with a few tweaks. 

You don't have to use my style, but I strongly recommend that you use a consistent style and you document it. If you're working on someone else's code, don't impose your own style. Instead, read their style documentation and follow it as closely as possible.

Good style is important because while your code only has one author, it will usually have multiple readers. This is especially true when you're writing code with others. In that case, it's a good idea to agree on a common style up-front. Since no style is strictly better than another, working with others may mean that you'll need to sacrifice some preferred aspects of your style.

The formatR package, by Yihui Xie, makes it easier to clean up poorly formatted code. It can't do everything, but it can quickly get your code from terrible to pretty good. Make sure to read [the notes on the website](http://yihui.name/formatR/) before using it. It's as easy as:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("formatR")
formatR::tidy_dir("R")
```

A complementary approach is to use a code __linter__. Rather than automatically fixing problems, a linter just warns you about them. The lintr package by Jim Hester checks for compliance with this style guide and lets you know where you've missed something. Compared to formatR, it picks up more potential problems (because it doesn't need to also fix them), but you will still see false positives.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("lintr")
lintr::lint_package()
```

### Object names

Variable and function names should be lowercase. Use an underscore (`_`) to separate words within a name (reserve `.` for S3 methods). Camel case is a legitimate alternative, but be consistent!  Generally, variable names should be nouns and function names should be verbs. Strive for names that are concise and meaningful (this is not easy!).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Good
day_one
day_1

# Bad
first_day_of_the_month
DayOne
dayone
djm1
```

Where possible, avoid using names of existing functions and variables. This will cause confusion for the readers of your code.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Bad
T <- FALSE
c <- 10
mean <- function(x) sum(x)
```

### Spacing

Place spaces around all infix operators (`=`, `+`, `-`, `<-`, etc.). The same rule applies when using `=` in function calls. Always put a space after a comma, and never before (just like in regular English).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Good
average <- mean(feet / 12 + inches, na.rm = TRUE)

# Bad
average<-mean(feet/12+inches,na.rm=TRUE)
```

There's a small exception to this rule: `:`, `::` and `:::` don't need spaces around them. (If you haven't seen `::` or `:::` before, don't worry - you'll learn all about them in [namespaces](#namespace).)

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Good
x <- 1:10
base::get

# Bad
x <- 1 : 10
base :: get
```

Place a space before left parentheses, except in a function call.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Good
if (debug) do(x)
plot(x, y)

# Bad
if(debug)do(x)
plot (x, y)
```

Extra spacing (i.e., more than one space in a row) is ok if it improves alignment of equal signs or assignments (`<-`).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
list(
  total = a + b + c, 
  mean  = (a + b + c) / n
)
```

Do not place spaces around code in parentheses or square brackets (unless there's a comma, in which case see above).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Good
if (debug) do(x)
diamonds[5, ]

# Bad
if ( debug ) do(x)  # No spaces around debug
x[1,]   # Needs a space after the comma
x[1 ,]  # Space goes after comma not before
```

### Curly braces

An opening curly brace should never go on its own line and should always be followed by a new line. A closing curly brace should always go on its own line, unless it's followed by `else`.

Always indent the code inside curly braces.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Good

if (y < 0 && debug) {
  message("Y is negative")
}

if (y == 0) {
  log(x)
} else {
  y ^ x
}

# Bad

if (y < 0 && debug)
message("Y is negative")

if (y == 0) {
  log(x)
} 
else {
  y ^ x
}
```

It's ok to leave very short statements on the same line:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
if (y < 0 && debug) message("Y is negative")
```

### Line length

Strive to limit your code to 80 characters per line. This fits comfortably on a printed page with a reasonably sized font. If you find yourself running out of room, this is a good indication that you should encapsulate some of the work in a separate function.

### Indentation

When indenting your code, use two spaces. Never use tabs or mix tabs and spaces. Change these options in the code preferences pane:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("images/style-options.png")
```

The only exception is if a function definition runs over multiple lines. In that case, indent the second line to where the definition starts:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
long_function_name <- function(a = "a long argument", 
                               b = "another argument",
                               c = "another long argument") {
  # As usual code is indented by two spaces.
}
```

### Assignment

Use `<-`, not `=`, for assignment.

```{r}
# Good
x <- 5
# Bad
x = 5
```

### Commenting guidelines

Comment your code. Each line of a comment should begin with the comment symbol and a single space: `# `. Comments should explain the why, not the what. \index{comments}

Use commented lines of `-` and `=` to break up your file into easily readable chunks.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Load data ---------------------------

# Plot data ---------------------------
```

title: Suggestion: comment style

`# ` for any comment

My suggestion:

`## ` for a full line comment
`# ` for a comment on a code line

Example:

```
## Example code
y <- 3 + 2          # I don't have imagination
```

Rationale:
- consistant with other style guides (e.g. https://www.bioconductor.org/developers/how-to/coding-style/)
- consistant with emacs comments
- allows auto-formatting options which indent and align single hashes, but do not indent double hashes (or indent them at the same level as surrounding code, depending on settings). This is very convenient!
- looks cleaner (this is so objective lol. I know :smile:)

Note: Jim Hester was ok to accept my PR to allow `## ` in `commented_code_linter` in the lintr package (see jimhester/lintr#301). So lintr is now happy with `## ` full line comments :grinning:

> To apply this style guide automatically, use lintr.

Should we add a reference to [styler](http://styler.r-lib.org), e.g. change the sentence to

> To apply this style guide automatically, use lintr for static code analysis and styler for reformatting code.

Or something like that?

title: Clarify spacing around bang-bang operators
description:
I think it would be useful to add an example under section [2.2 Spacing](http://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#spacing) on how spacing should be done around `!!!` and `!!`. In the [programming with dyplr](http://dplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/programming.html) vignette, there is no spacing around those operators whereas there is spacing around them in the help file for `rlang::quasiquotation` (up-to-date package version 0.1.2.9000).
Reference: https://github.com/krlmlr/styler/pull/110.

title: Line break and infix operators
description:
In [styler](https://github.com/krlmlr/styler/issues/255), we were wondering whether it would make sense to add a rule to the style guide that says
> If you use infix operators (such as `|`, `&` etc.) and you decide to break the line around them, the 
> line break should occur after the infix operator, not before it.
```r
# good
if (a_long_condition & and_another_long_condition &
  one_more) {
    # do something
}

# bad
if (a_long_condition & and_another_long_condition
  & one_more) {
    # do something
}
```

Or whether conditions should not be that long anyways so the problem does not occur and / or it is an edge case not worth mentioning.

In any case, we would probably implement a rule in styler that moves the infix operator one line up to change `# bad` above to `# good`.
cc: @krlmlr.

title: Documenting internal functions
description:
Should add a section about documenting internal functions which have no Rd files and are only intended to be read by other developers.

Recommendation is to use `#'` comments per usual, but with `@noRd` tag. See [Hadley's comment here](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/2210).

title: extending the style guide for roxygen2 documentation
description:
I was wondering whether it would make sense to extend the style guide with regard to `roxygen2` documentation, i.e. by giving guidelines on `roxygen2`-specific topics like :

* capitalisation of first letter in argument descriptions / bullet lists etc.
* Using or not using periods at the end of argument descriptions / bullet lists etc.
* Indention when description corresponding to a roxygen tag spans over multiple lines. 
* The order in which roxygen tags should be used.
* When to use `code_style_font` (only for functions, for variables, function arguments, TRUE / FALSE, NA etc.)?
* Whether to use `function_call()` or `function_call` when referring to a function.
* the use of data.frame, data frame or dataframe and the like.

I note that some conventions seem to exist, but even then it would make sense to turn the implicit into the explicit.

title: Mutate instead of sub assignment
description:
In a [PR](https://github.com/krlmlr/styler/pull/21) and a subsequent [issue](https://github.com/krlmlr/styler/issues/24) reviewed by @krlmlr, I was advised to avoid sub assignment when possible. I think I might be reasonable to extend the style guide in this regard, namely section 2.6.

```r
# Good
pd <- pd %>%
  indent_round(pd, indent_by = 2) %>%
  mutate(child = map(child, indent_round_nested)

# Bad
pd <- indent_round(pd, indent_by = 2)
pd$child <- map(pd$child, indent_round_nested)
```
What do you think?

title: Section 4.2 Spacing and indenting, "good" code is not correct
description:
```
iris %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarize_if(is.numeric(), mean) %>%
  ungroup %>%
  gather(measure, value, -Species) %>%
  arrange(value)
```
returns
```
Error in is.numeric() : 
  0 arguments passed to 'is.numeric' which requires 1
```
Correct code should be:
```
iris %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarize_if(is.numeric, mean) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  gather(measure, value, -Species) %>%
  arrange(value)
```

title: long lines
description:
[Long Lines](https://github.com/tidyverse/style/blob/master/04-pipes.Rmd#long-lines):
```r
iris %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarise(
    Sepal.Length = mean(Sepal.Length),
    Sepal.Width = mean(Sepal.Width),
    Sepcies = n_distinct(Species)
  ) %>%
  select(Species)
```
compare to

```r
iris %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarise(Sepal.Length = mean(Sepal.Length),
            Sepal.Width = mean(Sepal.Width),
            Species = n_distinct(Species)) %>%
  select(Species)
```

Matter of opinion, but I was just wondering what are the merits of the first one, esp. given that the second one is consistent with how [long line function args](https://github.com/tidyverse/style/blob/master/03-functions.Rmd#long-lines) are usually written.

title: Pipes style
description: @hrbrmstr had some good pointers re pipes in his [RStudio::conf talk](https://www.rstudio.com/resources/videos/writing-readable-code-with-pipes/), e.g. don't use the pipe for just one function (`mtcars %>% str()`), piping data into ggplot is probably not a good idea (breaks the pipes should be 'atomic' rule, etc.
